runs.analysis: The stage tweak requires: map each pitch field to a named ## section in a fixed order with Call to Action last, never turn why_this_pitch_works into a section, and prefer bullet lists over dense paragraphs. Candidate A follows all of this. It has no "Why This Pitch Works" section, it puts Call to Action last, and it breaks content into bullets and sub-bullets, so it is scannable. Candidate B breaks the explicit rules. It includes a "## Why This Pitch Works" meta-commentary section, which the tweak specifically forbids. It puts Call to Action in the middle instead of last. It leaves the Risks section and Long-term Vision as dense paragraphs. It also says "five dimensions" and then lists six, an internal inconsistency that A avoids by saying six. A has a few small issues. The title adds a "Connecting Continents" subtitle, and the Project Overview is still somewhat prose-heavy. Overall A is clearly better.

The stage's prompt tweak requires: map each pitch field to a named `##` section in a fixed order with `## Call to Action` last, never turn `why_this_pitch_works` into a section, and prefer bullet lists over dense paragraphs.

Candidate A breaks the first two rules. It includes a "Why This Pitch Works" section, which the tweak forbids because it reads as meta-commentary. It also puts Call to Action in the middle, not last. It leaves the Risks, Collaboration and Long-term Vision sections as dense paragraphs, which goes against the preference for bullets. It also says "five dimensions" and then lists six metrics, an internal inconsistency.

Candidate B follows the constraints. It has no why_this_pitch_works section, and Call to Action is last. It breaks risks, stakeholders, ethics and collaboration into bullets and sub-headings, so it is easier to scan. It correctly says "six dimensions". It has minor flaws: some Collaboration items are still paragraphs, and the Project Overview is a short paragraph. Both candidates carry the same content and the same questionable claims from the source pitch. B is clearly better.

The two candidates carry almost the same content, the same sections and the same facts: 60% take-or-pay, 25% ecological offset, 80% buffers, 75% local workforce, a 90-day ask and a Q4 2026 FID. Both end with Call to Action as the stage requires, and neither turns why_this_pitch_works into a section. The differences are about format.

A follows the "prefer bullet lists over dense paragraphs" instruction better. It turns Target Audience into a list and splits the Overview strategy into bullets. It also tones down the exclamation-heavy, hype-style prose, which suits the skeptical red-team context. Its weakness is the "(Decision N)" tags, which refer to internal decisions the reader can't see. In an investor-facing pitch they read as clutter. They do keep traceability to the raw JSON. A's Metrics section also has an awkward lead-in.

B keeps the Overview and Target Audience as dense paragraphs, which goes against the bullet-list instruction. Its tone is more promotional, with "Stop planning to maybe build...", an exclamation mark and "momentum toward national AI leadership". Its text is cleaner without the Decision tags, and it expands the PUE and FID acronyms, which helps a general reader. Section order differs between the two, and I can't tell which matches the fixed order.

Overall A complies slightly better with the prompt tweak and is a bit more scannable, so I give it a narrow edge.

The two candidates are nearly identical in content and section order. Both keep Call to Action last, and neither turns why_this_pitch_works into a section. Both reproduce the same raw-pitch claims (60% take-or-pay, 80% preserved footprint, 75% local workforce, Q4 2026 FID, binding RTE allocation before FID), so both inherit the same weak spots against the skeptical plan.

B follows the prompt tweak's preference for bullets better: it breaks the Project Overview strategy into bullets, where A leaves two dense paragraphs. A also adds hype that is not clearly in the source and runs against the plan's skeptical tone ("Stop planning to maybe build...", "We aren't guessing", "without bankrupting the venture", exclamation marks).

B's weakness is the "(Decision N)" tags. They appear to come from the raw JSON and keep the text traceable, but they mean nothing to an external pitch reader and clutter it. B also renames two sections and paraphrases the PUE metric less clearly. A has cleaner section names and states PUE directly.

The difference is small, and B edges ahead on bullet use and restraint.

Both candidates contain essentially the same content drawn from the raw pitch, follow the stage's structure (named ## sections, Call to Action last, no why_this_pitch_works section), and are faithful. Differences: A uses "(Decision 12)", "(Decision 1)", "(Decision 9)", "(Decision 10/2)" references. These are internal artifacts that make little sense to a pitch reader and clutter the text. A also leaves the Project Overview, Ethical, and Call to Action sections in dense paragraphs, which goes against the prompt tweak to prefer bullets over dense paragraphs. A's Call to Action is a paragraph. A adds slight embellishments ("Immediate, tangible benefits") and the "Stakeholder Benefits" section is placed before Risks. B uses bullets in the Call to Action and in the Collaboration and Long-term sections, uses a numbered list for metrics, and has a punchy hook ("Stop selling train tickets, start selling seamless journeys!"). That hook makes it more persuasive and better matches the "elevator pitch" purpose. B's Ethical Considerations is still a paragraph, and the benefits wording "with immediate, tangible benefits" is a little awkward. B has a minor oddity: it places Stakeholder Benefits after Metrics. The fixed section order is unknown, so neither can be faulted on that. Overall, B is cleaner, more scannable and more persuasive, and it follows the bullet preference better. A's Decision references are a real flaw.

Both candidates are complete and faithful to the same content. Candidate A follows the "prefer bullets over dense paragraphs" tweak much better: Risks, Long-term Vision, Call to Action and others are bulleted or numbered. Its section order looks like the natural pitch-field order (inferred, since the JSON isn't shown), it ends with Call to Action, and it opens with a strong hook. It has no internal jargon. Candidate B keeps several dense paragraphs (Risks, Long-term Vision, Call to Action). It leaks internal references such as "(Decision 12)", "(Decision 1)", "(Decision 9)" and "(Decision 10/2)", which mean nothing to the pitch's external audience. It also places Stakeholder Benefits ahead of Risks, which may deviate from the expected order. A is more scannable and polished.

The two candidates contain almost the same content. They share the same source quirks, such as "full €3.5M budget tranche" and the "triage script bypass". The differences come down to how well each follows the stage's formatting rules.

Candidate A puts `## Call to Action` last, as the stage tweak requires. It does not turn `why_this_pitch_works` into a section, and its Target Audience section is a plain list of audiences. Its weakness is that some sections, such as Stakeholder Benefits, Ethical Considerations and Collaboration Opportunities, are dense paragraphs. The tweak says to prefer bullets.

Candidate B breaks the fixed-order rule by placing `## Long-Term Vision` after `## Call to Action`. Its "Target Audience and Strategic Alignment" section includes "The pitch's strength lies in its alignment with…". This is the meta-commentary about the pitch that the tweak explicitly says to avoid. Its advantage is more consistent use of bullets and numbered lists, which makes it more scannable.

The tweak's explicit rules were call-to-action-last and no meta-commentary. B breaks both, so A follows the stage instructions better, despite B's better bullet use.

Both candidates convert the same pitch content into similar sections, with Call to Action last. The differences are in fidelity and in whether either one adds material.

Candidate A adds content that is not in the source pitch and that distorts it. It adds a "Target Audience and Strategic Alignment" paragraph, which is exactly the kind of meta-commentary about the pitch that the prompt tweak warns against ("The pitch's strength lies in..."). It adds the words "*guarantee*", "tested", "surgical" and "decisively". It also adds "Level 2+" and turns "Month 4 performance audit" into "full €3.5M". Some of this is in B too, because it comes from the source. Beyond that, A makes its own changes:
- It inserts "Immediate Resilience Deployment" into the title.
- It adds "Two critical pathways" to the Call to Action.
- It adds "mandatory two-person field teams".
- It adds "GDPR... to bypass immediate digital hurdles".
- It adds "Phase 1 procurement".

A also uses more bullet lists and bolding, which is more scannable, and it has a slightly different section order. Its "Target Audience and Strategic Alignment" section is wordy meta-commentary and a mild violation of the tweak.

Candidate B is more faithful and cleaner. It uses short sections, bullets in the Call to Action, and a closing line, "Our strategy is built on pragmatic controls, not ambition", that is a bit of flourish. Its Stakeholder Benefits section is paragraphs, not bullets, which is a small miss on "prefer bullets". Its Ethical Considerations and Collaboration sections are dense paragraphs, so it follows the bullet preference less well than A. A uses bullets in Collaboration and Stakeholder Benefits.

Both contain the same questionable claims from the source. Examples are the "triage script bypass", the premium-priced procurement, and the claim that the full €3.5M is released at Month 4, which is factually inconsistent with the plan's staged €2.0M + €1.5M. Neither candidate fixes these, and A repeats the €3.5M claim as well.

Overall, B is more faithful and has less meta-commentary. A is slightly more bullet-heavy but adds the meta-commentary section. I lean slightly toward B.
